**Dinosaurs' Roars May Have Been Mumbled, Not Roared**

New research suggests that dinosaurs may not have been as loud and ferocious as popularly depicted in movies. According to a study published online, some dinosaurs likely mumbled or cooed with their mouths closed, rather than roaring like the Tyrannosaurus Rex.

The researchers analyzed vocalizations of modern birds and reptiles, finding patterns between species size and body shape. They discovered that larger animals tend to use open-mouth vocalization while smaller ones prefer closed-mouth sounds. This pattern is consistent across different groups of archosauria including crocodilians and pterosaurs.

Closed mouth vocalization are more common among large bodied species because it allows for better resonance and amplification of sound waves within the neck cavity. NEWLINE_CHAR The team used statistical analysis on 208 bird species from around the world, which showed that this behavior evolved independently multiple times during evolution. 

This new understanding could change how we imagine Jurassic World. Instead of hearing T-Rex roars, we might hear softer murmurs or gentle coos. Gary Rydstrom, a renowned sound designer who worked on the original "Jurassic Park" film, has already experimented with creating dinosaur sounds using animal noises, such as geese hissing and dolphins clicking. He even slowed down recordings of whalesong to create an eerie, otherworldly effect.

While scientists can't directly observe what ancient creatures sounded like, they're working together to piece together clues about dinosaur communication. By studying living birds and reptiles, researchers hope to gain insights into the possible sounds made by non-avian dinosaurs. Future studies will integrate fossil evidence, physiological data, and computational modeling to recreate the lost voices of these prehistoric beasts.

In fact, recent discoveries suggest that many dinosaurs were feathered, had bulging necks, and possibly produced low-frequency rumbles through closed-mouth vocalizations. These findings challenge our traditional image of fierce, booming dinos and invite us to reimagine the sights and sounds of a long-lost era. As one researcher noted, "It's time to rethink the roar of the T-Rex."
details.ground_truth: Dinosaurs may have been much more like modern birds than we knew—and not just because some had feathers. A new study suggests that mighty dinosaurs of yore didn't roar, contrary to every dinosaur movie you've ever seen. Instead, they made a decidedly less scary sound called a "closed-mouth vocalization." Think of a dove cooing or perhaps an ostrich doing this grunting thing. As the scientists explain in the journal Evolution, per UT News, the sound actually comes out of the neck area after air is pushed through an esophageal pouch. In fact, the animal's mouth is shut the whole time. Lots of birds do this today, and because birds descended from dinosaurs, scientists suspect they may have communicated in a similar way. The fossil record can't prove it, though the Washington Post notes that previous research meshes with the idea, including the belief that dinosaurs had air sacs instead of vocal chords. “A cool thing about this work is the demonstration that closed-mouth behavior evolved many times,” says the lead author. “That suggests it can emerge fairly easily and be incorporated into mating displays" among different types of animals. A co-author says the study gives the impression of "a very different Jurassic world. Not only were dinosaurs feathered, but they may have had bulging necks and made booming, closed-mouth sounds." But if so, the makers of Jurassic Park didn't get it all wrong: The hiss of the film's velociraptors came from a goose, per Vulture. (Scientists have grown chickens with dinosaur legs.)

"It's a symbol that is, for many people, deeply offensive and painful," Zeppos told the Tennessean. Efforts by Middle Tennessee State University in Murfreesboro to remove the name of Confederate Gen. Experts predict that Tsarnaev's execution could take at least 10 years, given the complexity of the case and potential lines of appeal.

Only 62 inmates currently sit on federal death row, with many having been convicted of crimes related to public violence or domestic terrorism. In contrast, almost half of these inmates were put there by just three states: Texas, Missouri, and Virginia.

As Tsarnaev begins his long journey through the appeals process, questions surround whether justice can truly be served when the system moves so slowly. **$8.2 Billion Merger: IntercontinentalExchange to Acquire NYSE Euronext**

In a major deal, IntercontinentalExchange Inc. (ICE) is set to acquire the New York Stock Exchange's parent company, NYSE Euronext, in an $8.2 billion takeover. The merger marks a significant shift in the global market for derivatives and stocks.

According to sources briefed on the matter, ICE will offer approximately $33 per share of NYSE Euronext stock, with two-thirds of that amount being paid in stock. This represents a 37% premium over the exchange's closing price on Wednesday.

The acquisition highlights the growing importance of derivatives trading, which has eclipsed traditional stock trading. While the iconic New York Stock Exchange has been synonymous with American capitalism for centuries, its businesses in over-the-counter derivative trading have become increasingly attractive to investors.

NYSE Euronext's electronic Arca platform accounts for around 12% of all US stock trades, while the average number of daily traded shares has declined every year since 2009. In contrast, futures and options trading volumes have fallen less significantly.

By acquiring NYSE Euronext, ICE would gain access to one of the industry's fastest-growing exchanges, boasting high profit margins. The combined entity would own 14 stock and futures exchanges, as well as five clearing operations, making it the largest player in the financial markets.

Regulatory approval and shareholder support are still required before the deal can be finalized. However, if successful, this merger would mark a new era in the evolution of financial markets, cementing the dominance of electronic trading over traditional floor-based systems.

Other potential bidders or opponents, including CME Group and rival exchanges from Hong Kong and Singapore, may express concerns about antitrust implications or nationalist interests. Nevertheless, the proposed transaction appears poised to reshape the landscape of global finance.

In response to growing criticism about its lack of diversity, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Science has taken a significant step towards increasing representation within its ranks. Jordan, and Regina King; as well as international heavyweights like Hou Hsiao-Hsien and Souleymane Cissé.

In recent years, there have been several high-profile campaigns calling attention to the lack of diversity in Oscar nominations, culminating in the #OscarsSoWhite hashtag created by April Reign.

details.ground_truth: Apparently still smarting from some of Chris Rock's Oscars barbs, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences invited 683 people—many of them women and minorities—to join in an unprecedented move Wednesday, Reuters reports. The voting group behind the Oscars is largely old, white, and male and was lambasted this year with the hashtag #OscarsSoWhite after two years in a row of all-white acting nominees. In response, the academy is attempting to—as the AV Club puts it—" add seemingly goddamn everyone it had, for one reason or another, forgotten to invite into its membership.” The actors, directors, and others invited Wednesday include Idris Elba, Eva Mendes, Oscar Isaac, John Boyega, Ice Cube, Greta Gerqig, Michael B. Using the scans they were then able to reproduce the videos—though they’re blurry. “This is a major leap,” the co-author says. details.ground_truth: Forget satellite images and aerial searches—the best way to find Malaysia Airlines Flight MH370 may be with mathematical techniques dating back to the 18th century, the BBC reports. That's how Air France flight 447 was found in 2009, using "Bayesian statistics" to measure the probability of the plane being in one place or another. Named after Presbyterian minister and mathematician Thomas Bayes, the technique allowed experts to apply several factors to each point on a map: For example, what was the chance it crashed from mechanical failure? How far do planes tend to crash from their last known location? What was the chance that search teams missed debris in various locations? It's like picking a restaurant by balancing how full it is, what your favorite restaurant-review website says, and so on—except that experts hunting for Airbus A330 did that for each point where plane may have crashed in the Atlantic, Five Thirty-Eight notes. It was so hard that the US team of statisticians invited by France gave up, until they de-emphasized one statistic: that a plane's black box emits a signal after a crash 90% of the time. They changed their findings, and presto, the plane was found. Bayesian techniques have helped people find World War II U-boats, men overboard, and sunken treasure, but there's no evidence that Malaysia is employing them now. "I suspect that they just guess, like professional baseball managers used to do before Moneyball," says a biostatistician.

**Rare Super Blue Blood Moon Eclipse on January 31, 2018**

On January 31, 2018, a rare celestial event will occur: a total lunar eclipse that coincides with the second full moon in a single month (known as a blue moon) and is also considered a supermoon. This phenomenon has not occurred for over 150 years.

The eclipse will be visible from eastern Asia to western North America, with the best views available from Australia, New Zealand, and parts of Eastern Europe. The Virtual Telescope Project will provide a live stream of the event, allowing people around the world to witness this spectacular sight remotely.

A supermoon occurs when the moon is at its closest point to Earth, making it appear larger and brighter than usual. In this case, there are three consecutive supermoons occurring between December 3, 2017, and February 1, 2018. However, having three supermoons in a row is extremely rare.

During the lunar eclipse, the moon will take on a reddish hue due to the way light passes through the Earth's atmosphere. NASA recommends capturing photos or videos of the event using smartphones or DSLR cameras, suggesting tips such as locking focus, adjusting exposure settings, and incorporating context into your shots.

While special glasses are required to view solar eclipses safely, viewers can watch the supermoon and lunar eclipse without any protective gear. Simply find a clear spot outside or tune in online to experience one of the most unique astronomical events of our time.

Key details:

* Date: January 31, 2018
* Time: Begins at 11:48 am UTC; peak visibility at 2 pm UTC
* Visibility: Eastern Asia to Western North America, with optimal viewing areas including Australia, New Zealand, and Eastern Europe.
* Live Stream: Available via the Virtual Telescope Project website.
details.ground_truth: Look up at the sky on Jan. 31 and you may witness a sight unseen for 150 years. For the first time since 1866, a total lunar eclipse will occur with the blue moon, or second full moon of the month, which—like the one visible on New Year's Day—will also be a supermoon. Got all that? When the moon is at or near the closest point to Earth in its orbit (aka, a supermoon), it appears 14% bigger and 30% brighter than full moons that occur at the farthest point in the moon's orbit, though the moon will lose brightness as it enters Earth's shadow, according to NASA. Because of the way Earth's atmosphere bends light, the eclipsed moon will take on a reddish hue, something often referred to as a blood moon, making this rare celestial event "a super blue blood moon eclipse," according to the Miami Herald. The next blue moon eclipse won't occur until 2028. The eclipse will last for 3.5 hours, with the total eclipse stretching for 77 minutes, reports Sky & Telescope. Those along the Pacific Rim from Alaska and northwestern Canada to central and eastern Asia, Indonesia, New Zealand, and Australia will get the best view of totality during the middle of the night. However, partial phases of the eclipse should be visible under a clear sky in central North America, western Asia, India, the Middle East and eastern Europe, per Space.com. North American viewers should look up as the moon sets on the morning of Jan. 31, while those on the opposite side of the world should see a partial eclipse as the moon rises. Not in an ideal viewing area? The Virtual Telescope plans to livestream the total eclipse from Australia, which you can watch here, per Quartz. (Bogus glasses damaged a solar eclipse viewer's eyes.)

**Syria Protests Escalate: US Ambassador Visits Hama, Thousands Demonstrate**

The situation in Syria continues to deteriorate as protests against the government of President Bashar al-Assad intensify. On Friday, over 500,000 people gathered in the city of Hama, which has become a symbol of opposition since the 1982 crackdown on protesters by Assad's father.

In an effort to show support for the Syrian people, US Ambassador Robert Ford visited Hama on Thursday and met with local residents. The visit was seen as a significant gesture of solidarity, but it also sparked criticism from the Syrian government, which accused Washington of interfering in its internal affairs.

Despite the presence of security forces, thousands of protesters took to the streets in Hama on Friday, carrying olive branches and chanting slogans calling for democracy and freedom. However, reports indicate that at least 13 protesters were killed across the country, including three in the city of Hasrata just outside Damascus.

The violence is part of a larger pattern of repression by the Assad regime, which has been criticized for its brutal response to peaceful demonstrations. Human rights groups estimate that hundreds have died in recent weeks, while thousands more have been arrested or forced into hiding.

The international community remains divided on how to respond to the crisis. While some countries, such as France, have called for greater action to pressure the Assad regime, others are urging caution and restraint.

Meanwhile, the United States has condemned the violence and expressed concern about the humanitarian situation in Syria. State Department officials say they will continue to provide assistance to those affected by the conflict and call for an end to the bloodshed.

As tensions remain high, there are fears that the situation could escalate further, potentially leading to wider instability in the region. For now, however, the focus remains on supporting the Syrian people and pushing for a resolution to the crisis through diplomatic means.

Key Developments:

* Over 500,000 people protested in Hama on Friday
* At least 13 protesters killed across the country
* US Ambassador Robert Ford visits Hama, sparking criticism from the Syrian government
* Violence reported in several cities, including Hasrata near Damascus
* International community remains divided on how to respond to the crisis
* US condemns violence and expresses concern about humanitarian situation in Syria
details.ground_truth: America's ambassador to Syria visited one of the cities worst-hit by the crackdown against anti-government protesters yesterday, reports CNN. Robert Ford went to the city of Hama "to make absolutely clear with his physical presence that we stand with those Syrians who are expressing their right to speak for change," an embassy spokeswoman says. An estimated 500,000 people joined an anti-government rally in the city last Friday. The Syrian government accused Ford of going to the city without authorization, saying the visit is "clear evidence of the US involvement in the ongoing events in Syria and its bids to aggravate the situations which destabilize Syria.'' An embassy spokeswoman says the Syrian government was told a delegation would be visiting Hama, although no Syrian "handlers" were taken and officials weren't informed about the ambassador's presence. The city has been a symbol of opposition since 1982, when a crackdown ordered by the present Syrian leader's father killed around 20,000 people, al-Jazeera notes.

**Election Security Threats on the Rise: FBI Investigates Attempt to Hack Democratic National Committee's Voter Database**

As the US heads into midterm elections, concerns about election security and foreign meddling have reached a fever pitch. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is investigating an attempt by hackers believed to be tied to Russian intelligence to breach the voter database of the Democratic National Committee (DNC). However, in a surprising twist, it was later revealed that what initially appeared to be a sophisticated hacking attempt was actually an unauthorized "simulated phishing test."

The incident highlights the ongoing threat posed by cyber attacks aimed at manipulating electoral processes. Microsoft reported this week that its systems detected attempts by Russian-backed hackers to target the Senate and conservative think tanks in the United States through fake websites.

Experts warn that the focus has shifted from stealing secrets to using cyber tools to impose national power. With many voting registration systems vulnerable to manipulation, there are numerous opportunities for both domestic and foreign actors to interfere with the democratic process.

In response to these threats, government organizations and political groups have been put on high alert ahead of the midterms. Facebook recently identified a disinformation campaign targeting people around the world, while Twitter announced measures to combat misinformation on its platform.

Security experts emphasize the need for vigilance in preventing future attacks. As Bob Lord, chief security officer for the DNC, noted, "This attempt is further proof that there are constant threats as we head into midterm elections... We must remain vigilant in order to prevent future attacks."
details.ground_truth: The FBI is reportedly investigating a sophisticated—but unsuccessful—attempt to hack into the Democratic National Committee's voter database. The DNC learned of the attempt on Tuesday, CNN reports. The attack, which was detected by a cloud service provider and a security research company, involved a fake login page intended to gather usernames and passwords for a service called Votebuilder, which hosts the DNC's voter database. It's a method called "spearphishing," according to the New York Times. "It was very convincing," Mike Murray of the cybersecurity firm Lookout tells CNN, adding that it would be tough to tell the real page from the fake one, even if they were side-by-side. The fake login page was ultimately removed by the cloud hosting company DigitalOcean. The company's chief security officer says the threat was identified before the attack was launched. "We see no evidence that any sensitive data was stolen," he says. A DNC official tells the Times that it is not clear who the hackers were in this case. But, the paper recalls, a 2016 hack of the DNC was ultimately traced to Russia. This latest attempt, DNC Chief Security Officer Bob Lord tells the Times, "is further proof that there are constant threats as we head into midterm elections and we must remain vigilant in order to prevent future attacks." Earlier this week, Microsoft reported that it had uncovered new Russian hacking attempts targeting conservative organizations in the US.

**Boston Marathon Bombing: A City in Mourning**

In the aftermath of Monday's devastating Boston Marathon bombings, a city is reeling from the loss of three innocent lives. The victims have been identified as Martin Richard, an 8-year-old boy from Dorchester; Krystle Campbell, a 29-year-old restaurant manager from Medford; and Lu Lingzi, a Chinese graduate student at Boston University.

The explosions occurred just before 3 p.m., near the finish line on Boylston Street, killing two people immediately and injuring hundreds more. In the chaos that followed, a family was mistakenly told their daughter had survived when she actually did not. Krystle Campbell's parents were later informed of her passing by hospital officials.

As investigators work to identify those responsible for the attack, FBI officials assure there are no known additional threats against the city. Mayor Thomas Menino has vowed that Boston will "not be intimidated" by terrorism and will come together to heal and move forward.

Meanwhile, residents and visitors alike continue to show solidarity with the families affected by the tragedy. Neighbors left flowers outside the home of victim Martin Richard, while others participated in vigils and prayer services across the city.

President Obama praised first responders and the resilience of the American spirit, saying, "If you want to know who we are, look at how we respond." As the nation comes together to support Boston, the city remains strong in its resolve to overcome evil and rebuild.

A memorial service is planned for Thursday, where President Obama will attend alongside other dignitaries. In the meantime, the community continues to mourn the losses suffered during this senseless act of violence.
details.ground_truth: Another fatality in the Boston bombings has been identified: The family of 29-year-old Krystle Campbell says she was killed as she and a friend were cheering on another friend who was racing, reports WCVB. "This is just a waste," says her mother. “Everyone that knew her loved her. She was always smiling. You couldn’t ask for a better daughter. She was the best.” Campbell was a restaurant manager, reports the Boston Herald, which notes an especially wrenching detail: Her father was initially told she was alive, but when he got to the ICU, he realized it was his daughter's friend who had survived. Campbell is the second of the three people killed to be identified. The first was 8-year-old Martin Richard, and his father, Bill, released a statement today thanking supporters and asking for privacy, reports WBZ. "My dear son Martin has died from injuries sustained in the attack on Boston. My wife and daughter are both recovering from serious injuries. We thank our family and friends, those we know and those we have never met, for their thoughts and prayers. I ask that you continue to pray for my family as we remember Martin. We also ask for your patience and for privacy as we work to simultaneously grieve and recover. Thank you." The third victim was a grad student at Boston University, but the person's identity is being withheld until the family says it's OK to release, reports USA Today.

**Global Obesity Epidemic: A Growing Concern**

A recent study published in the Lancet medical journal has revealed a staggering 2.1 billion adults worldwide are either obese or overweight, with obesity rates soaring by nearly 30% over the past three decades. The United States leads the world in obesity numbers, but it's far from alone - every country is struggling to combat this growing public health crisis.

According to researchers at the University of Washington and the World Health Organization (WHO), no nation has successfully reduced its obesity rate since data collection began in 1980. In fact, the problem is most acute in developing countries, where two-thirds of the global population resides. The Middle East region saw particularly high increases in obesity rates, with Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Oman, Kuwait, and Egypt experiencing significant rises.

The WHO reports that almost one-third of all adults globally now suffer from obesity or being overweight, which significantly raises their risk for heart disease, stroke, diabetes, and certain types of cancer. Children and adolescents are also increasingly affected, with obesity rates rising by nearly 50% worldwide during the same period.

Interestingly, while developed nations like the US have seen slowing growth in adult obesity rates over the past eight years, women in these regions tend to be more severely impacted than men. Conversely, men in developing countries experience higher obesity rates than women.

Notably, just ten countries account for more than half of the world's obese population: the United States, China, India, Russia, Brazil, Mexico, Japan, Germany, France, and Italy. These findings highlight the urgent need for coordinated international efforts to address this pressing issue.

As Dr. Marie Ng, lead researcher on the project, notes, "Obesity is not just an aesthetic concern; it's a major risk factor for chronic diseases." With the number of people suffering from obesity projected to continue increasing unless drastic measures are taken, governments, healthcare professionals, and individuals must work together to develop effective solutions to mitigate this epidemic.

Sources:

* USA Today
* Reuters
* World Health Organization (WHO) report
details.ground_truth: There are more obese or overweight people in the world today than there were people of any weight in 1935, the most comprehensive look at worldwide obesity in decades warns. The 188-country study found that there are 2.1 billion overweight or obese people in the world, making up around 30% of the world's population, up from 20% in 1980, USA Today reports. Not a single country has recorded a decline in obesity over the last 30 years. "We hoped there would be some examples of success that you could latch onto," a study co-author says. "But there's a complete lack of success stories in bringing down obesity." The study published in British medical journal the Lancet found that the Middle East and north Africa had seen the biggest weight gains, though the US still has the largest number of obese people, with 87 million of the world's 671 million obese people, reports Reuters. Other countries, however, have even higher obesity rates, including Tonga, where more than 50% of all adults are obese. "Two-thirds of the obese population actually resides in developing countries," says one of the researchers; they warn that obesity rates are rising among rich and poor countries, men and women, and adults and children alike.

details.ground_truth: It's been a year since Katie Holmes filed for divorce from Tom Cruise, and apparently Cruise is feeling sentimental. A source tells UK magazine Look the actor sent Holmes an "emotional letter" looking to, at the very least, be friends again, Australia's News Network reports. "It's like he's finally recognized that Katie will always be the love of his life," the source says. Even so, "It won't have been an over the top letter—it has been a year and I'm sure Tom will have been aware that Katie wouldn't be interested in running straight back into his arms." **LOCAL NEWS SUMMARY**

A bizarre incident occurred in Mendon on Wednesday evening when a car was suspended from a telephone pole's guy wire after the driver reacted too quickly to GPS directions. Nabila Altahan, who was driving a Toyota Corolla with her passenger, lost control of the vehicle while westbound on Route 4 and ended up stuck on the wire support across from Sugar & Spice Restaurant.

According to police reports, the GPS device instructed Altahan to turn around as she had passed her intended destination, prompting her quick reaction that led to the accident. Fortunately, neither Altahan nor her passenger were injured in the incident.

The Rutland City Fire Department and State Police responded promptly to the scene, which drew attention from witnesses at nearby businesses, including a miniature golf course where one witness reported seeing the driver jump out of the car as it became lodged on the pole.

This unusual incident serves as a reminder for drivers to exercise caution when following GPS instructions, especially during unexpected situations or changes in traffic conditions.
details.ground_truth: Police in Vermont say a car ended up almost vertical when the driver swerved quickly in response to her GPS ordering her to "turn around." The car was suspended almost vertically on guide wires attached to a utility pole (see a photo here) in Mendon on Wednesday night, reports the AP. Police say 30-year-old Nabila Altahan of Dorchester, Mass., was headed west on US Route 4 when she passed her intended destination and reacted quickly to the instructions, leaving the road at a significant enough speed to propel the vehicle up the wires. She wasn't injured. (This driver followed her GPS into a lake.)
